guarantees.claim: When rst_ni is low (reset active), err_q is forced to 0 immediately.
When not in reset and either intg_err or reg_we_err is high at a rising clock edge, err_q becomes 1 on the next clock cycle.
Otherwise (no reset and no error condition), err_q retains its previous value.

assumptions.claim: rst_ni is assumed to be a clean asynchronous reset signal that meets standard recovery/removal timing and is asserted for at least one full clock cycle.
assumptions.cond: during reset deassertion or when err_q is expected to be cleared
assumptions.risk: If rst_ni is glitchy or not held long enough, err_q may not clear properly, retaining a stale error that could propagate to downstream security logic.

formal_sketch.antecedent: during reset deassertion or when err_q is expected to be cleared
formal_sketch.consequent: rst_ni is assumed to be a clean asynchronous reset signal that meets standard recovery/removal timing and is asserted for at least one full clock cycle

uncertain_points.claim: err_q is sticky and never cleared by this block except on reset. It is unclear whether a software-clear or auto-clear mechanism exists elsewhere; if absent, a single error latches err_q permanently until system reset.
uncertain_points.cond: After any error event (intg_err || reg_we_err) has set err_q
uncertain_points.risk: Permanent error state may deny service or mask subsequent error events, affecting HMAC integrity monitoring.

formal_sketch.antecedent: After any error event (intg_err || reg_we_err) has set err_q
formal_sketch.consequent: err_q is sticky and never cleared by this block except on reset. It is unclear whether a software-clear or auto-clear mechanism exists elsewhere; if absent, a single error latches err_q permanently until system reset

security_implications: err_q is a sticky error indicator for integrity errors (intg_err) and register write errors (reg_we_err) in the HMAC register block. If this flag cannot be cleared without a system reset, an attacker could deliberately trigger an integrity error to permanently lock the error signal, potentially blinding the system to further errors or forcing an unrecoverable fault state.
